title: SAP Cloud Integration: an MCP server that lets AI agents build and test iFlows
author: DamianKolasa

title: From Business Intent to AI Agents: A Practical Guide to Getting Started with SAP Joule Studio
author: pvsbprasad
text:
Introduction 
 The way we build enterprise applications is evolving. Traditionally, developers started with requirements, designed the architecture, identified APIs, wrote code, performed testing, and finally deployed the solution. 
 With the evolution of Agentic AI, this development approach is changing. 
 SAP Joule Studio introduces Intent-Based Development (IBD), enabling developers to move from describing a business requirement in natural language to generating, testing, and deploying an AI agent. 
 Instead of manually starting with every technical implementation detail, developers can describe the desired business outcome. Joule Studio assists with requirements discovery, solution architecture, technical specifications, code generation, testing, and deployment. 
 In this blog, let's explore how to get started with SAP Joule Studio and understand the complete development journey, from defining an intent to deploying your first AI agent. 
 1. Understanding SAP Joule Studio 
 SAP Joule Studio provides an environment for developing enterprise AI agents. 
 Its Intent-Based Development approach allows developers to: 
 Describe business requirements using natural language. 
 Discover relevant SAP capabilities and APIs. 
 Generate a Product Requirements Document (PRD). 
 Create technical specifications and architecture. 
 Generate agent implementation code. 
 Test and evaluate agent behavior. 
 Deploy agents to the SAP Managed Runtime Service. 
 The objective is to simplify agent development while ensuring that the resulting solution is aligned with SAP architecture, business processes, and enterprise requirements. 
 Joule Studio provides a web-based developer experience. Developers can also use the Joule Studio CLI with their preferred development tools. Both approaches follow the same development workflow and deploy to the same managed runtime. 
 2. Prerequisites: Setting Up Joule Studio 
 Before starting development, the required Joule Studio environment must be provisioned. 
 The initial setup is primarily handled by the system administrator. 
 Administrator checklist 
 Step 1: Provision Core Components 
 Provision the Core Components blueprint through SAP for Me. This establishes the foundational services and tenants required for subsequent provisioning. 
 Step 2: Provision Joule 
 Provision the Joule blueprint and connect it to the relevant SAP systems, such as SAP S/4HANA Cloud, SAP SuccessFactors, SAP LeanIX, and other applicable systems. 
 Step 3: Provision Joule Studio 
 Provision the Joule Studio blueprint. This establishes the developer environment and connects the Agent Gateway and other integrations. 
 Step 4: Assign Developer Roles 
 In SAP Cloud Identity Services, assign the JouleStudioDeveloper group to the developer's user account. 
 Step 5: Configure Git for Production 
 For production deployments, configure the GitHub connection with OIDC trust between SAP Cloud Identity Services and GitHub. 
 Git configuration is not required to start development and testing in the development environment. 
 Understanding the key roles 
 Role Responsibility 
 Joule Studio Developer Create, edit, deploy, and monitor own solutions 
 Joule Studio Administrator View, deploy, and monitor all tenant solutions 
 Joule End User Access Joule Work and interact with deployed agents 
 Once the environment is ready, developers can access Joule Work and navigate to Develop → Joule Studio . 
 3. Key Concepts Behind Joule Studio 
 Before creating an agent, it is important to understand the intelligence and runtime components that support Intent-Based Development. 
 3.1 Agentic Development 
 Agentic Development goes beyond traditional AI-assisted coding. 
 Instead of simply suggesting code snippets, AI agents can assist with multiple stages of the development lifecycle. 
 In Joule Studio, developers describe the intended business outcome, and the platform assists with discovery, architecture, implementation, and deployment. 
 3.2 SAP Knowledge Graph – AI-Driven Discovery 
 SAP Knowledge Graph plays an important role in discovering relevant SAP capabilities. 
 It helps map the developer's business intent to SAP's Reference Business Architecture, identify relevant APIs and their specifications, and perform Fit-Gap Analysis. 
 This helps determine: 
 What functionality is already available in standard SAP. 
 Which APIs and capabilities can be reused. 
 Where custom development may be required. 
 3.3 SAP Domain Models – SAP-Specific Intelligence 
 SAP Domain Models provide enterprise and SAP-specific knowledge to support solution recommendations. 
 They combine SAP-purpose-built domain models with third-party large language models and leverage application code, process knowledge, and industry expertise. 
 This helps validate proposed solutions against SAP best practices. 
 3.4 SAP LeanIX – Enterprise Landscape Context 
 SAP LeanIX provides visibility into the customer's actual enterprise architecture. 
 It provides context about: 
 Existing SAP systems. 
 Deployment models. 
 Integrations. 
 Enterprise architecture and organizational structures. 
 This allows Joule Studio to consider the customer's existing IT landscape rather than relying only on a generic reference architecture. 
 3.5 Joule Studio Runtime 
 Joule Studio Runtime is SAP's managed execution environment for enterprise agents, supporting applications, and workflows. 
 SAP manages the underlying runtime infrastructure, including execution, scaling, connectivity, operations, and observability. 
 Developers can focus on defining business logic, policies, integrations, and expected outcomes. 
 4. Intent-Based Development: The Six-Stage Workflow 
 Now let's explore the most important part: creating your first AI agent. 
 Intent-Based Development follows six major stages: 
 Intent 
 Requirements 
 Specification 
 Solution 
 Testing 
 Deployment 
 The workflow is iterative. Developers can revisit previous stages and refine the solution based on the generated outputs and testing results. 

 Step 1: Define Your Business Intent 
 Navigate to: 
 Joule Work → Develop → Joule Studio → Create 
 Start by describing what you want the agent to accomplish. 
 A good intent statement should clearly communicate: 
 What the agent should do. 
 Which SAP systems or business data it should connect to. 
 Which business persona it serves. 
 What output or action is expected. 
 What business outcome should be achieved. 
 Example: 
 "An AI-powered Customer Billing Agent that helps customers and business users retrieve billing information, check invoice details, understand payment status, identify overdue invoices, and resolve billing-related queries using SAP business data. Build an agent. Fast Track. start with intent-analysis" 
 Once the intent is submitted, Joule starts asking clarifying questions to understand the business requirements, constraints, and expected outcomes. 
 AI-Driven Discovery 
 Behind the scenes, Joule Studio uses different intelligence components: 
 SAP LeanIX provides enterprise landscape context. 
 SAP Knowledge Graph discovers relevant APIs and maps capabilities to SAP Reference Business Architecture. 
 SAP Domain Models provide SAP-specific architectural guidance. 
 Fit-Gap Analysis identifies standard SAP coverage and potential custom development requirements. 
 Based on this discovery, Joule presents a proposed solution along with an intent fit percentage. 
 Developers can refine the proposed solution through the Joule chat before proceeding. 
 Once satisfied, select Create Requirements . 

 Step 2: Review the Product Requirements Document (PRD) 
 Joule Studio generates a Product Requirements Document based on the defined intent and discovery process. 
 The PRD includes: 
 Business context and value proposition. 
 User personas and user stories. 
 Functional requirements and acceptance criteria. 
 High-level solution architecture. 
 API references identified through the Knowledge Graph. 
 In-scope and out-of-scope requirements. 
 Why is PRD review important? 
 This is one of the most important checkpoints in the development process. 
 Before moving forward, validate whether the generated requirements accurately represent the business scenario. 
 Check whether: 
 All business requirements are covered. 
 The user stories reflect actual business needs. 
 The proposed architecture is appropriate. 
 The identified APIs are relevant. 
 The scope and limitations are clearly defined. 
 If something is incorrect or missing, refine it through the Joule chat. 
 Once satisfied, select Create Specs . 

 Step 3: Review the Technical Specification 
 After the PRD is approved, Joule Studio generates the Technical Specification. 
 This translates business requirements into a technical implementation blueprint. 
 It includes: 
 Architecture decisions and design patterns. 
 Data model and integration design. 
 SAP API connections, endpoints, authentication, and usage patterns. 
 Security and compliance considerations. 
 Prioritized implementation tasks. 
 At this stage, developers should validate the technical feasibility of the proposed solution. 
 Pay particular attention to API availability, authentication requirements, connectivity, and the target SAP environment. 
 Do not proceed until the technical design aligns with the actual implementation requirements. 
 Once validated, select Create Solution . 

 Step 4: Generate the Solution (Code) 
 Based on the approved Technical Specification, Joule Studio generates the agent implementation code. 
 Developers can review the generated files and project structure in the Code tab. 
 The generated implementation can be refined by describing the required changes through the Joule chat. 
 For example: 
 Modify the agent's business logic. 
 Refine decision-making instructions. 
 Correct tool invocation behavior. 
 Adjust the handling of specific business scenarios. 
 An important consideration is that AI-generated code must be reviewed just like code contributed by another developer. 
 Review the implementation, validate the generated logic, and ensure that it follows the intended business and technical requirements. 

 Step 5: Test Your AI Agent 
 Testing is essential before deploying an AI agent. 
 Joule Studio automatically runs unit tests and AI-powered evaluations. 
 Developers can review the results in the Testing view and interact with the agent through the Preview interface. 
 Validate the following: 
 Does the agent understand the requests made by end users? 
 Does it invoke the correct tools? 
 Are tools executed in the correct sequence? 
 Does it handle invalid inputs and edge cases? 
 Are business rules and conditional logic applied correctly? 
 If the agent does not behave as expected, identify the relevant instruction or tool, refine the implementation, and execute the tests again. 
 The objective is not simply to ensure that the agent responds, but to validate that it performs the intended business task correctly and consistently. 

 Step 6: Deploy to Joule Studio Runtime 
 Once the agent passes the required validation, it is ready for deployment. 
 Click the Deploy button in Joule Studio. 
 All supported solution types follow a unified deployment process to the SAP Managed Runtime Service. 
 SAP manages the underlying infrastructure and scaling, eliminating the need for developers to manage the runtime infrastructure themselves. 
 After deployment, developers can validate the agent through Joule Work. 

 Monitoring and Observability 
 Deployment is not the end of the development lifecycle. 
 Joule Studio provides monitoring capabilities through AI Agent Hub. 
 Key capabilities include: 
 Solution List: View deployed agents and their status. 
 Artifact List: View the components associated with a solution. 
 Activity / Trace: Inspect step-by-step execution traces for individual agent interactions. 
 Monitoring Dashboard: Review usage information and performance metrics.

title: Transportable CSRF token handling in SAP API Management without an API provider in the callout
author: VikasSingh2
text: A CSRF token fetch in SAP API Management that refers to the API proxy itself. It reuses the provider and connection the proxy already has, works with OAuth and an API key in front, and moves from DEV to QA to UAT to PRD without a new API provider.
